stages.title: Rules, Scoring & the Court
stages.description: How a badminton match is scored under the BWF Laws, when players change ends, what the court and net look like, and when a shuttle is in or out.
learningObjectives: Explain rally-point scoring, the two-point rule and the cap for a game, and best-of-three matches

explainBack.question: Explain how a badminton game and match are won under the current BWF Laws, what changes from January 2027, and how you decide if a shuttle that lands on a line is in.
rubric: Every rally wins a point; under the Laws in force until 3 Jan 2027 a game goes to 21, at 20-all a side needs a two-point lead, and at 29-all the 30th point wins
A match is best of three games; there is a 60-second interval when the leader reaches 11, up to 120 seconds between games, and ends change after each game and at 11 in game three
From 4 Jan 2027 BWF games go to 15 points: two-point lead from 14-all, cap at 21 (20-all next point wins), interval and third-game change of ends at 8
The court is 13.4 m long, 6.1 m wide for doubles and 5.18 m for singles; the net top is 1.524 m at the centre and 1.55 m over the doubles side lines
Lines are part of the area they define, so a shuttle landing on the line is in; it is a fault if it lands outside, fails to cross the net, or a player touches the net

explainBack.question: A friend is starting badminton. Explain which shuttles they might use and why, and how to hold the racket for forehand and backhand shots.
rubric: Feather shuttles have 16 feathers (usually goose or duck) in a cork base and weigh about 4.74-5.50 g; they are used in serious competition
Synthetic/plastic shuttles last much longer than feathers (which may need replacing every few games), so they suit schools and casual play; their flight differs from feathers
Forehand grip: a handshake hold with a V formed between thumb and index finger, used for forehand overheads, drives, lifts and net shots
Backhand grip: rotate so the thumb presses flat on the wide back of the handle, used for backhand drives, lifts, net shots, serves and doubles defence
Hold the racket loosely with relaxed fingers so you can change grips quickly mid-rally

Backhand grip: thumb on the wider part of the handle
Bevel grip for backhand rear-court shots; panhandle for some net kills
Fingers stay loose so grips can change quickly

stages.title: Serving
stages.description: The service laws, the singles and doubles service courts, and how to play low and high serves.

explainBack.question: Explain what makes a serve legal, where you serve from and to, and when you would choose a high serve versus a low serve in singles.
rubric: The whole shuttle must be below 1.15 m from the court surface when hit, the racket must first hit the base of the shuttle, and the racket must keep moving forward
Server and receiver stand in diagonally opposite service courts without touching the lines, with part of both feet on the floor and stationary until the serve is delivered
Serve from the right court when the server's (or serving side's) score is even and from the left when it is odd

The singles service court is long and narrow (to the back boundary, singles side line); the doubles one is short and wide (to the long service line 0.76 m inside the back, doubles side line); both start at the short service line 1.98 m from the net
The high serve goes high and deep so the shuttle drops steeply near the back line; the low serve skims the net to land just past the short service line and stops the receiver attacking

explainBack.question: Describe how you should stand and move to reach a shuttle in a front corner and a rear corner, and what you do after hitting it.
rubric: Ready position: feet slightly wider than shoulders, knees bent, weight on the balls of the feet, racket held in front of the body
Split step: a small jump timed just before the opponent hits so you land balanced and push off quickly
Movement follows a cycle of start, approach, hit and recover, using steps such as chassé, running steps and lunges
Front-corner lunge: lunge with the racket leg, heel landing first and knee over the foot, torso upright
Rear corners: chassé back and use a scissor jump, then recover towards the central base for the next shot

explainBack.question: Name the six core badminton strokes and, for each, describe where it sends the shuttle and when you would use it.
rubric: Clear: an overhead shot hit high and deep to the opponent's back court; a high clear buys time, a flatter attacking clear pressures an out-of-position opponent
Drop: a soft shot that slows the shuttle so it lands in front of the service line near the net, pulling the opponent forward
Smash: a fast, steep, downward overhead shot and the main attacking stroke

Net shot: played from forecourt to forecourt as close to the net top as possible, bringing the opponent forward; the lift sends the shuttle from forecourt to the rear court, high to defend or lower to attack
Drive: a fast, flat shot just over the net, mostly in the midcourt, used to attack or defend

explainBack.question: Describe a basic game plan for a singles rally: where you aim, where you go after each shot, and how you create an opening to win the point.
rubric: Hit towards the four corners because it makes the opponent cover the most distance and pulls them away from their central base
After each shot recover towards a central base, which sits slightly behind the middle of the court and shifts forward after net shots and back after clears or lifts
Split step as the opponent hits so you can move in any direction
Use deep, high serves and length to push the opponent back, and vary tempo unexpectedly
Keep overhead preparation identical (disguise) so the opponent cannot read clear, drop or smash, and deceive them into moving the wrong way

explainBack.question: Explain how a doubles pair should position themselves when attacking and when defending, how they switch, and why most doubles serves are low.
rubric: Attack: front-back formation; the rear player smashes or drops while the front player covers the net and finishes weak replies
Defence: side-by-side formation covering the full court width, standing about a step behind the middle of the court
When the pair lifts they move from front-back to side-by-side; when they get a chance to hit down, one player moves forward to make front-back
The low serve is used most because it starts falling below net height soon after crossing, making it hard to attack; aim at the T, with an occasional flick serve
After a high serve the serving pair defends side-by-side and the receiving pair attacks, with the receiver's partner moving to the front

stages.title: Fitness, Injury Prevention & Training
stages.description: What injuries badminton players commonly get, the main risk factors, and how warm-ups, load management and structured drills reduce them.
learningObjectives: Identify the most common badminton injury locations and types

explainBack.question: What injuries are badminton players most likely to get, what raises the risk, and how should a club player warm up and structure training to reduce it?
rubric: Most badminton injuries (41-92% in a 2025 systematic review) affect the lower body, especially ankle/foot and knee; the upper limb is the next most affected
Common types include sprains and strains, plus overuse problems such as tendinopathy and stress fractures; Achilles tendon ruptures make up about 3-8.7% of acute badminton injuries
Previous injury and higher competition level raise injury risk; fatigue is linked with Achilles ruptures, which mostly happen mid- or late game
Warm up before playing (the NHS suggests at least about 6 minutes, e.g. marching, knee lifts, shoulder rolls), and stop if you feel pain
Increase training load gradually rather than in sudden jumps, and use structured drills such as multi-feed practice to build badminton-specific endurance and consistency

Sprains and strains are the most common acute injuries; overuse 25-74%
Main risk factors: higher competition level and previous injury
Rapid increases in training load cause many injuries

resources.title: A narrative review of Achilles tendon ruptures in racket sports

keyPoints: Achilles ruptures are about 3-8.7% of acute badminton injuries
87% of badminton ruptures happened mid- or late game
Fatigue and sudden acceleration/deceleration are implicated
Most players return to sport within 12 months with structured rehab
